seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

msIdentifier.repository: Manuscripts and Archives Division, New York Public Library

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: I have not received the copy of your Poems nor that of Poetry with my verses and Mr. Eliot’s verses, nor the advance from Mr. Quinn which you mention in yours of 17th ult. What is the date of his letter to you? In his last to me (7 ult) he says nothing of it. I hope you are well. Am alone here. Wife and children gone to Lago Maggiore . Will write you in a few days about your proposition of some months ago concerning Ulysses . Have written to Yeats about Exiles . Mr. G_____ promised to read it.

div.note: This is a typed transcription of a missing original, mentioned and enclosed with a letter from Ezra Pound to John Quinn of 23 August 1917. Obvious mistypings have been silently corrected.

Pound wrote on 17 July 1917 that JJ would receive a copy of Pound’s volume of poems, Lustra, set to appear in the fall of 1917 in New York. It contained, among other poems, “Three Cantos of a Poem of Some Length,” revised from their appearance in Poetry, vol. 10, nos. 3-5 (June, July, August 1917): 113-21, 180-88, 248-54. See JJ to Pound, 24 July 1917, notes.

The Chicago-based magazine Poetry printed JJ’s poems “Simples,” “Tutto è Sciolto,” “Flood,” “A Flower Given to My Daughter,” and “Nightpiece” as a group in the May 1917 issue, and “On the Beach at Fontana,” “Alone,” and “She Weeps over Rahoon” in the November 1917 issue. These poems, with revisions, were all collected in Pomes Penyeach (1927).

“The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock” by T.S. Eliot (1888-1965) first appeared in Poetry, vol. 6, no. 3 (June 1915): 130-35. His volume of poems, Prufrock and Other Observations, was published in June 1917 by the Egoist Press in an edition partially subsidized by Ezra and Dorothy Pound. JJ received his copy on 22 October 1917 (LIII 510).

John Quinn (1870-1924), a collector of modern art and literary manuscripts, had arranged to purchase items from JJ, including the manuscript of his play Exiles and the setting copy used for the American edition of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (1916) (see JJ to Pound, 19 March 1917, notes). Pound wrote on 17 July 1917 that Quinn had sent JJ “an advance” on the Exiles manuscript (Pound/Joyce 121). When Quinn finally received acts two and three of Exiles, he sent JJ, on 18 August 1917, a “Zurich draft for 522.50 francs, being the equivalent of £25,” which did not reach JJ until mid-September (Myron Schwartzman, “‘Quinnigan’s Quake!’ John Quinn’s Letters to James Joyce, 1916-1920,” Bulletin of Research in the Humanities, vol. 81, no. 2 [Summer 1978]: 231).
JJ was planning to winter with his family in Locarno, on the northern shore of Lago (Lake) Maggiore, and had sent Nora Barnacle and their two children ahead. See JJ to Pound, 24 July 1917, notes.

With plans to serve as foreign editor of The Little Review (New York), Pound had written JJ on 19 April 1917 and in other letters that he wanted to serialize Ulysses in the magazine (Pound/Joyce 111). Ulysses was partially serialized in The Little Review (1918-1920) before being issued as a book in February 1922 in Paris by Sylvia Beach’s Shakespeare and Company and also, in October 1922, by the Egoist Press of London.

JJ hoped that W.B. Yeats (1865-1938) would persuade the Dublin Abbey Theatre to produce Exiles, but Yeats wrote JJ on 26 August 1917 that the play was “a type of work we have never played well” since it was “too far from the folk drama.” He thought it “[not] at all so good” as A Portrait (LII 405).

Probably J.T. (Jacob Thomas) Grein (1862-1935), an influential theatre producer and critic in London who JJ hoped would help get his play Exiles staged. JJ asked his literary agent J.B. Pinker on 8 August 1917 to send Grein, at that time in Devon, a typescript copy of Exiles (LII 401-02). See also JJ to Pound, 30 March 1917, notes.
